options: A. Leave the canoe behind and race each other swimming to shore.

B. Stay with the floating canoe (which has built-in foam flotation blocks), move to the upwind side, and perform a canoe-over-canoe rescue with their buddy boat or flip/paddle the swamped canoe to shore.
C. Stand up on top of the overturned hull to wave both arms.
D. Tie the bow painter line around their waists while floating on the downwind side of the hull.

pamphlet_excerpts: Upper Side Rail Gunwales: Gunwales (pronounced "gunnels") are rails that run along the top edge of both sides of the canoe (p. 27).
Hull Strength and Shape Retention: Gunwales add strength to the hull and help it keep its shape (p. 27).
Crosswise Thwart Support Braces: Braces, called thwarts (pronounced "thorts"), span the width of the canoe and provide rigidity and support (p. 27).
Centerline Bottom Keel Ridge: Some canoes also have a small keel, a ridge that runs the length of the bottom of the canoe along its center line (p. 27).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Inspect Crosswise Thwart Braces: Braces, called thwarts (pronounced "thorts"), span the width of the canoe and provide rigidity and support (p. 27).
Step 2 - Locate the Centerline Keel Ridge: Some canoes also have a small keel, a ridge that runs the length of the bottom of the canoe along its center line (p. 27).
Step 3 - Balance Tracking Against Turning Ease: A keel improves a canoe's ability to travel in astraight line but hinders its ability to turn (p. 27).
Step 4 - Identify Ahead and Astern Directions: When you are facing forward in your canoe, ahead is the direction in front of the bow, and astern is the direction behind the boat (p. 27).

pamphlet_excerpts: Lower Center of Gravity: In the kneeling position, the paddler's center of gravity is lower than in the seated position (p. 38).
Increased Stability When Kneeling: This puts the paddler in a more stable position in the boat (p. 38).
Leaning Against Seat or Thwart: When kneeling in the canoe, the paddler should sit up straight with their buttocks leaning against the seat or thwart behind them (p. 38).
Proper Back and Leg Alignment: Avoid kneeling with the back and upper legs in alignment (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Rest Against Seat or Thwart: When kneeling in the canoe, the paddler should sit up straight with their buttocks leaning against the seat or thwart behind them (p. 38).
Step 2 - Avoid Straight Vertical Kneeling Posture: Avoid kneeling with the back and upper legs in alignment (p. 38).
Step 3 - Shift Knee Into Hull Curve: The body should be slightly shifted to the paddling side of the paddler so the knee is in the curved part of the hull (p. 38).
Step 4 - Place Closed-Cell Foam Knee Pad: A kneeling cushion or pad of closed cell foam is almost always needed for the kneels even for short trips (p. 38).

C. It lowers their center of gravity and puts the canoe in a more stable position
D. It allows them to use a much longer paddle than when standing up
choices: A. It raises their center of gravity so they can see farther downstream

requirements.lead_text: With a companion, using a properly equipped canoe to demonstrate the following tandem maneuvers while paddling in unison on opposite sides and without changing sides. Each paddler must demonstrate these maneuvers in both the bow and stern and on both sides of the canoe while maintaining trim and balance of the canoe:
requirements.req_text: With a companion, using a properly equipped canoe to demonstrate the following tandem maneuvers while paddling in unison on opposite sides and without changing sides. Each paddler must demonstrate these maneuvers in both the bow and stern and on both sides of the canoe while maintaining trim and balance of the canoe: (a) Pivot (spin) the canoe 180° (half circle) to the right from a stationary position, stop, and return to the starting position by pivoting to the left using draw and pushaway strokes or using forward and reverse sweeps staying within 2 boat lengths of the starting position. (b) Move a canoe sideways (abeam) in one direction for 10 feet and then return to the starting position using the draw and pushaway strokes. (c) While in forward motion, stop the canoe within two boat lengths using the backstroke. (d) While in the stern position and without assistance from the bow paddler, paddle in a straight line 15-20 boat lengths using an appropriate steering stroke, e. g., the J-stroke or thumb-down rudder stroke with or without a stern pry. (e) Move the canoe in a straight line 15-20 boat lengths with the bow paddler using as necessary the forward stroke, draw stroke or forward sweep and the stern paddler using an appropriate steering stroke, e. g., the J-stroke or thumb-down rudder stroke with or without a stern pry. (f) While maintaining forward motion, turn the canoe 90° in an arc to the right in 5-10 boat lengths with the bow paddler using as necessary either the draw stroke or forward sweep and the stern paddler using only the forward stroke. Repeat the maneuver turning the canoe 90° to the left. (g) Move the canoe backwards in a straight line 3-4 boat lengths using as necessary the back stroke, reverse sweep or draw stroke in the bow or the stern. (h) Complete a figure of 8 course around markers 3-4 boat lengths apart using appropriate strokes including the draw stroke, and the forward and reverse sweeps.

requirements.description: With a companion, using a properly equipped canoe to demonstrate the following tandem maneuvers while paddling in unison on opposite sides and without changing sides. Each paddler must demonstrate these maneuvers in both the bow and stern and on both sides of the canoe while maintaining trim and balance of the canoe: (a) Pivot (spin) the canoe 180° (half circle) to the right from a stationary position, stop, and return to the starting position by pivoting to the left using draw and pushaway strokes or using forward and reverse sweeps staying within 2 boat lengths of the starting position. (b) Move a canoe sideways (abeam) in one direction for 10 feet and then return to the starting position using the draw and pushaway strokes. (c) While in forward motion, stop the canoe within two boat lengths using the backstroke. (d) While in the stern position and without assistance from the bow paddler, paddle in a straight line 15-20 boat lengths using an appropriate steering stroke, e. g., the J-stroke or thumb-down rudder stroke with or without a stern pry. (e) Move the canoe in a straight line 15-20 boat lengths with the bow paddler using as necessary the forward stroke, draw stroke or forward sweep and the stern paddler using an appropriate steering stroke, e. g., the J-stroke or thumb-down rudder stroke with or without a stern pry. (f) While maintaining forward motion, turn the canoe 90° in an arc to the right in 5-10 boat lengths with the bow paddler using as necessary either the draw stroke or forward sweep and the stern paddler using only the forward stroke. Repeat the maneuver turning the canoe 90° to the left. (g) Move the canoe backwards in a straight line 3-4 boat lengths using as necessary the back stroke, reverse sweep or draw stroke in the bow or the stern. B. Stay with the floating canoe (which has built-in foam flotation blocks), move to the upwind side, and perform a canoe-over-canoe rescue with their buddy boat or flip/paddle the swamped canoe to shore.
C. Stand up on top of the overturned hull to wave both arms.
D. Tie the bow painter line around their waists while floating on the downwind side of the hull.
choices: A. Leave the canoe behind and race each other swimming to shore.

B. Stay with the floating canoe (which has built-in foam flotation blocks), move to the upwind side, and perform a canoe-over-canoe rescue with their buddy boat or flip/paddle the swamped canoe to shore.
C. Stand up on top of the overturned hull to wave both arms.
D. Tie the bow painter line around their waists while floating on the downwind side of the hull.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Stay with the floating canoe (which has built-in foam flotation blocks), move to the upwind side, and perform a canoe-over-canoe rescue with their buddy boat or flip/paddle the swamped canoe to shore.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Shorelines look much closer than they are across open water; staying with the buoyant canoe on the upwind side prevents wind drift separation and enables rapid buddy recovery.

choices: A. Completing the distance in one continuous swim without stops and making at least one sharp turn

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Completing the distance in one continuous swim without stops and making at least one sharp turn
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): To qualify as a swimmer for canoe operation, you must jump feetfirst into deep water and complete the 100 yards in one continuous swim without stops, including at least one sharp turn (p. 9).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does a centerline keel on the bottom of a canoe affect its handling on the water?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a centerline keel on the bottom of a canoe affect its handling on the water?
options: A. It makes the hull turn sharply in whitewater but prevents straight-line paddling
B. It improves the canoe's ability to travel in a straight line but hinders its ability to turn
C. It replaces the need for gunwales and thwarts along the upper edges of the hull
D. It raises the paddler's center of gravity so the canoe glides faster in shallow mud
choices: A. It makes the hull turn sharply in whitewater but prevents straight-line paddling
B. It improves the canoe's ability to travel in a straight line but hinders its ability to turn
C. It replaces the need for gunwales and thwarts along the upper edges of the hull
D. It raises the paddler's center of gravity so the canoe glides faster in shallow mud
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It improves the canoe's ability to travel in a straight line but hinders its ability to turn
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): A keel is a ridge along the bottom centerline that helps a canoe track straight ahead in wind or open water, though it makes pivoting and turning more difficult (p. 27).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why do experienced canoeists kneel with their buttocks resting against the seat or thwart rather than sitting high on the seat in rough water?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why do experienced canoeists kneel with their buttocks resting against the seat or thwart rather than sitting high on the seat in rough water?
options: A. It raises their center of gravity so they can see farther downstream
B. It keeps their back and upper legs locked in a vertical line without touching the hull
C. It lowers their center of gravity and puts the canoe in a more stable position
D. It allows them to use a much longer paddle than when standing up
choices: A. It raises their center of gravity so they can see farther downstream
B. It keeps their back and upper legs locked in a vertical line without touching the hull
C. It lowers their center of gravity and puts the canoe in a more stable position
D. It allows them to use a much longer paddle than when standing up
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. It lowers their center of gravity and puts the canoe in a more stable position
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Kneeling while leaning against the seat or thwart lowers the paddler's center of gravity and wedges the knee into the curve of the hull for superior stability (p. 38).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which type of whistle is recommended as a sound signal device for canoeing?
options: A. A chrome-plated metal whistle with a cork ball inside
B. A pealess plastic whistle that will not corrode or jam when wet
C. A brass referee whistle attached to the canoe's stern line
D. Any whistle containing a small metal ball inside the chamber
choices: A. A chrome-plated metal whistle with a cork ball inside
B. A pealess plastic whistle that will not corrode or jam when wet
C. A brass referee whistle attached to the canoe's stern line
D. Any whistle containing a small metal ball inside the chamber
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. A pealess plastic whistle that will not corrode or jam when wet
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Paddlers should choose an inexpensive, well-made plastic whistle without a ball, because metal whistles can corrode and internal balls can get stuck in the chamber (p. 15).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How often should wooden gunwales, seats, and thwarts on a canoe be oiled as part of routine maintenance?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How often should wooden gunwales, seats, and thwarts on a canoe be oiled as part of routine maintenance?
options: A. Only once every five years when the wood splits
B. Before every single launch while the wood is wet
C. At least twice a year after cleaning off sand and debris
D. Never, because oil softens wooden thwarts and gunwales
choices: A. Only once every five years when the wood splits
B. Before every single launch while the wood is wet
C. At least twice a year after cleaning off sand and debris
D. Never, because oil softens wooden thwarts and gunwales
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. At least twice a year after cleaning off sand and debris
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Along with wiping out sand and mud after each trip and storing the hull upside down under cover, you should oil wooden gunwales, seats, and thwarts at least twice a year (p. 30).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why should you never step into a canoe that has one end resting on the shore or dock and the other end floating in the water?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why should you never step into a canoe that has one end resting on the shore or dock and the other end floating in the water?
options: A. It traps air under the keel and causes the canoe to float away too fast
B. It creates an unstable bridged canoe that can tip over or damage the hull when loaded
C. It violates the 100-yard swimmer classification rule for flatwater launches
D. It forces the paddler to keep both hands free of gear while boarding
choices: A. It traps air under the keel and causes the canoe to float away too fast
B. It creates an unstable bridged canoe that can tip over or damage the hull when loaded
C. It violates the 100-yard swimmer classification rule for flatwater launches
D. It forces the paddler to keep both hands free of gear while boarding
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It creates an unstable bridged canoe that can tip over or damage the hull when loaded
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Having one end on shore and the other floating bridges the hull; a bridged canoe is unstable and stepping into it can injure the paddler or damage the boat (p. 37).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What should paddlers bring along when launching a canoe from shore to rescue a distressed swimmer who is beyond the reach of a throw bag?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What should paddlers bring along when launching a canoe from shore to rescue a distressed swimmer who is beyond the reach of a throw bag?

choices: A. Only a small sponge so the canoe stays as light as possible

C. Extra wooden thwarts to brace the swimmer across the gunwales
D. An extra flotation aid, such as a spare lifejacket, that can be handed to the swimmer
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. An extra flotation aid, such as a spare lifejacket, that can be handed to the swimmer
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When using a canoe as a rescue craft for a distressed swimmer beyond shore throw-line reach, paddlers should carry a flotation aid such as an extra lifejacket to give to the swimmer (p. 86).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why should a canoeist keep their hands within the imaginary 'paddler's box' and rotate their torso during each stroke?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why should a canoeist keep their hands within the imaginary 'paddler's box' and rotate their torso during each stroke?
options: A. It isolates the small wrist muscles so the back and core do not have to work
B. It protects the shoulder joints from unstable positions and uses strong torso muscles to prevent fatigue
C. It allows the paddler to lean far outside the gunwales without wearing a lifejacket
D. It eliminates the need for steering strokes like the J-stroke or sweep stroke
choices: A. It isolates the small wrist muscles so the back and core do not have to work
B. It protects the shoulder joints from unstable positions and uses strong torso muscles to prevent fatigue
C. It allows the paddler to lean far outside the gunwales without wearing a lifejacket
D. It eliminates the need for steering strokes like the J-stroke or sweep stroke
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It protects the shoulder joints from unstable positions and uses strong torso muscles to prevent fatigue
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Staying within the paddler's box keeps shoulder joints in safe, stable positions, while rotating the torso recruits the large muscles of the trunk to power strokes and reduce fatigue (p. 51).
